story980:
The Pawnee believe that after death, the soul travels along the Milky Way, which they call the Great Medicine Road or the Path of the Dead. This celestial road leads the deceased to the land of the dead, a place of eternal peace and plenty.

The journey is long and difficult. The soul must cross vast distances of sky, navigating by the stars that Tirawa placed as guides. Along the way, the soul encounters obstacles — rivers of darkness, mountains of silence, forests of shadow. But the stars light the path, and the songs of the ancestors guide the way.

The Milky Way was not merely a poetic image for the Pawnee — it was a literal road, a path that the soul walked after death. The brightest stars were rest stops, places where the soul could pause and gather strength. The darkest patches were dangerous stretches where the soul needed courage.

The land of the dead was not a paradise but a continuation of life. The people there hunted, planted, danced, and sang just as they had on earth. The difference was that there was no suffering, no disease, no old age. The dead lived in their prime, forever young, forever strong.

The Great Medicine Road was the Pawnee's way of understanding death — not as an ending but as a journey. The soul did not cease to exist when the body died. It simply moved to a different place, following a road that had been waiting since the beginning of time.
story981:
Shakuru (the Sun) and Pah (the Moon) were the last of all gods placed in the heavens by Tirawa. They are of relatively minor standing in Skidi Pawnee mythology compared to the star gods. The Sun and Moon are secondary lights — necessary for life but not as powerful as the stars.

Shakuru was the Sun — bright, warm, life-giving. He drove across the sky each day in his chariot, his rays bringing light to the world. But Shakuru was also harsh and demanding. His heat could dry the rivers, burn the crops, and drive people mad.

Pah was the Moon — gentle, cool, mysterious. She followed Shakuru across the sky each night, her silver light illuminating the darkness. But Pah was also fickle. She waned and grew, disappeared and returned, her moods as changeable as the tides.

Together, Shakuru and Pah governed the rhythms of day and night, the cycle of months, the alternation of light and darkness. They were the visible face of Tirawa — the aspect of the Creator that the people could see and touch.

The Skidi Pawnee observed the movements of the Sun and Moon with the same precision they applied to the stars. They tracked the solstices and equinoxes, predicted eclipses, and marked the passage of time by the phases of the Moon. The Sun and Moon were not merely religious figures — they were astronomical instruments, their movements providing the data that governed agricultural and ceremonial life.
story982:
A Comanche hunting party was pursuing a herd of antelope across the plains when a strange antelope with glowing eyes appeared. The lead hunter recognized it as a spirit messenger and halted the chase.

The spirit antelope spoke: "The people have hunted too much. The land is tired. The game is dwindling. You must return to your village and give thanks for what you have."

The hunters were frightened but obedient. They returned to the village and told the elders what the spirit had said. The people gathered for a ceremony of thanksgiving, offering tobacco to the spirits and praying for the return of the game.

The antelope spirit appeared again, this time in a vision to the medicine man. It taught him the songs of renewal — songs that would restore the balance between the people and the land. The medicine man performed the songs, and the game returned.

The story teaches that the spirits are watching, that the land has limits, and that the people must live in balance with the natural world. Taking too much from the land invites consequences, and only through gratitude and respect can the cycle of abundance continue.
